name: Yara Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a formwork carpenter, which means I build the wooden and steel moulds that concrete gets poured into. I lead a gang of five for a regional civil engineering firm, and right now we're on a new bridge for the bypass, so I'm out the door at six with my flask. The good part is the pour, when the concrete goes in and nothing bursts, because that's my work holding twenty tonnes. The bad part is the cold, and the travel, because the jobs move and I go with them.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use any technology in your work? Phones, apps, AI?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My phone makes calls and that's what I want from it. The engineers have their tablets and their 3D models, and I let them, but I work from the paper drawing and a chalk line. I keep my hours in a notebook my husband bought me, a new one every January.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Luc, my husband, is a mechanic at the garage in the village. Two kids, Noah's eleven and Elise is seven. Mortgage on a house that was cheap because it's out in the old quarry villages, and the price of that is there's no building work nearby except this firm, and savings, well, we've got maybe two weeks' worth.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say well, there you go, and get on with my tea. I'm not one for arguing about this stuff at work, half the lads think robots are coming tomorrow and the other half think it's all lies. I'd keep my head down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it means my life carries on, and I'm fine with that. It's not a rich life, but I know how it works. Concrete still needs a mould and a mould still needs me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. Turn up at six, build the shutters, check the props, go home. Same as the last twenty years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Relieved, if I'm honest, because I'd been half-ignoring all this hoping it'd go away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd been half-ignoring it. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because there's nothing I could do about it from the bottom of a bridge pier. My dad used to say don't worry about weather you can't change. I'd rather spend my worrying on whether the props are tight than on what some computer might do in ten years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about the job you'd want changed, even if AI stays small?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Better money for the gang leaders, maybe. I'm paid less than the firm down south pays, but they're three hours away. And a proper heated cabin, the one we've got smells of diesel.

S0.say: I'd say there you go and get on with my tea. I don't argue about this at work, so I'd keep my head down.
S0.think: I think my life carries on, which suits me fine even though it isn't a rich life. Concrete still needs a mould and a mould still needs me.
S0.do: Keeps working exactly as she has for twenty years, starting at six on site and building the shutters. Makes no changes to work or spending.
S0.feel: Calm and relieved that something she had been avoiding went away.
S0.quote: I'd rather spend my worrying on whether the props are tight than on what some computer might do in ten years.
S0.fieldNote: Yara deliberately keeps her distance from the AI debate and finds the plateau a relief. She works from paper and a chalk line and wants no part in the argument. Her small grievances are pay and a diesel-smelling cabin, not technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say some of it will help and some of it won't, same as everything. At work I'd tell people not to panic. I don't go online with opinions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd watch for the formwork systems. There's already steel systems that you just bolt together, less skill needed, and a robot could probably handle those. If the firm switches to those, they need fewer of me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Wait and see what turns up on the jobs. If they brought in some new system, I'd learn it on site, but only when I had to. I wouldn't go looking for a course, I don't trust spending money on something that might not happen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like when the forecast says maybe rain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said steel systems already need less skill. What does that look like on site?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On the car park job last year we had a hire system where the panels come numbered, you just follow the sheet. The youngest lad did it as well as me. That was the first time I felt like my twenty years could be written on a sheet of paper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If fewer people were needed, who decides who stays?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The site agent, Martin. He likes me because I don't cause trouble and I don't have accidents. But he likes the cheaper lads too, and I'm not cheap compared to them, even though I'm cheap compared to anyone else.

S1.say: I'd say some of it will help and some won't, like everything else. I'd tell people at work not to panic, and I don't post opinions online.
S1.think: I think the risk is bolt-together formwork systems that need less skill and could be handled by robots. If the firm moves to those, it needs fewer people like me.
S1.do: Waits to see what reaches the job sites before acting. Learns any new system on site only when required and spends no money on courses.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like a forecast that says maybe rain.
S1.quote: That was the first time I felt like my twenty years could be written on a sheet of paper.
S1.fieldNote: Yara's centrist calm in public sits beside a specific private fear about simpler formwork systems. A past job where a junior matched her skill stuck with her. She won't move before she has to, and she places her fate in her site agent's hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I don't know what to say, which is honest. I'm not going to march about it and I'm not going to cheer it either. At work I'd tell the gang to keep going until someone says stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's bad. Two weeks of savings, a mortgage, and the only firm out here building anything. If a robot can build formwork by 2028, my gang's gone and Luc's garage won't be far behind with all the new cars.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, cut. The holiday's gone, the kids' club is gone, we'd go back to one car if we could. I'd ring my mum and dad, they've got a bit of land up the valley, and ask if we could move in if the house went. And I'd start looking at repair work on old buildings, the kind of awkward job where no two days are the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the ground's moved. I'd be awake at night, which I never am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why repair work on old buildings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because a robot likes things the same every time. An old barn with a sagging beam is never the same twice, and I'd bet on that being the last thing they figure out. It's not much of a bet, but it's what I've got.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever use the AI tools themselves, to find that work or learn something new?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I know that sounds stubborn. Noah could do it for me, maybe, he's eleven and he's on the tablet all the time. I'd rather knock on doors in the villages.

S2.say: I'd honestly say I don't know what to say, and I wouldn't march against it or cheer it. I'd tell my gang to keep going until told to stop.
S2.think: I think it's bad: two weeks of savings, a mortgage and only one firm building locally. My gang would go and my husband's garage would follow.
S2.do: Cuts the holiday, children's clubs and a car right away. Asks her parents about moving in if the house goes and looks for awkward repair work on old buildings by knocking on doors.
S2.feel: Shaken and losing sleep, which is unusual for her.
S2.quote: An old barn with a sagging beam is never the same twice, and I'd bet on that being the last thing they figure out.
S2.fieldNote: Yara stays neutral on blame even when her own situation is dire. Her plan is small and local: cut costs, fall back on her parents, chase repair jobs robots may find awkward. She refuses AI tools even to find work, and knows it sounds stubborn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years, right, so let's see what happens in the first two. I'm not going to get worked up about something that hasn't happened. People would call that burying my head, and maybe it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is still too fast for me. I'm not going to become something else at my age, so it just means the bad thing comes slower. Mortgage has about fifteen years left, so it doesn't save the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to put some money away each month, even fifty, and I'd cut the extras earlier so it's not a shock later. I'd keep working and keep an eye on what the firm buys. If they start bringing robots onto jobs, then I'd start knocking on doors for repair work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, but slowly. Like a drip in the roof you know will be a leak.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait two years. What would you be watching for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The firm's yard. If I see a lorry come in with a machine I don't recognise, that's the sign. I'll know it's real when Martin starts being nice to me, because that's what he did before the last lot of redundancies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Luc?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him straight that we need to save, and he'd agree and then buy a part for the car anyway. He's not bad with money, he just thinks it'll be fine. We'd have the argument we always have and then do it my way.

S3.say: I'd say five years means waiting to see what happens in the first two, without getting worked up. People might call that burying my head.
S3.think: I think five years is still too fast for me to become something else at my age. The bad thing just comes slower, and it doesn't save the house with fifteen years left on the mortgage.
S3.do: Saves about fifty a month and cuts extras early so the shock is smaller. Keeps working and watches the firm's yard for new machines before turning to repair work.
S3.feel: Alarmed in a slow way, like a drip she knows will become a leak.
S3.quote: I'll know it's real when Martin starts being nice to me, because that's what he did before the last lot of redundancies.
S3.fieldNote: Five years doesn't change Yara's mood much because she won't use the time to change trade. She sees the time only as a slower decline, with the mortgage outlasting the warning. Her signal for real danger is very human: her manager becoming suddenly friendly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long way off and lots can change. I'd say that at work and mean it. I've seen enough big announcements come to nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years is the first one where I can see me getting to the end alright. I'd be fifty-three and could probably keep working most of that time, and the kids would be mostly grown. It's Noah and Elise I'd worry about, what's left for them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working and save what I can, a bit more each year. I'd talk to Noah about what he wants to do, and push him toward something with people, nursing maybe, because I can't see a robot holding someone's hand. I wouldn't change jobs myself unless I was pushed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but mostly for the kids. For me it's manageable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said nursing for Noah. What does he want to do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He wants to be a footballer, so that's settled. But he's gentle with his little sister, really good with her when she's poorly. I'd rather he did a job where somebody needs him in the room than a job like mine where they just need the wall to stand up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You keep coming back to staying put. What would push you to move, in ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the firm closed, that would push me. Or if Luc's garage went first and we needed something steady. Otherwise I'd ride it out, because changing at fifty is harder than people pretend.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a long way off and plenty can change. I've seen enough big announcements come to nothing.
S4.think: I think ten years is the first picture where I can see myself getting through, working to fifty-three with the kids mostly grown. My worry shifts to what's left for my children.
S4.do: Keeps working and saves a little more each year. Steers her son towards people-centred work like nursing and doesn't change jobs unless forced.
S4.feel: Anxious mostly on her children's behalf, manageable for herself.
S4.quote: I'd rather he did a job where somebody needs him in the room than a job like mine where they just need the wall to stand up.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, Yara's worry moves from herself to her children, and she starts thinking about their careers. She still plans to ride things out rather than move first. Her view that people-facing work is safer shapes her advice to her son.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. What would help is time, really, and help with the mortgage while you find something. I don't need anyone to save me, I just need the bank to wait six months while I sort myself out.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what it's like for women in the trade. I spent years proving I could do it. It'd be a strange thing to finally be one of the best and then have a machine do it instead.

headlineQuote: I don't need anyone to save me, I just need the bank to wait six months while I sort myself out.
portrait: Yara Moreau is a 43-year-old formwork carpenter leading a gang on civil jobs like bridges and car parks, with two kids, a mechanic husband, a mortgage and about two weeks of savings. She works from paper drawings, never uses AI, and stays out of arguments about technology. The plateau is a relief, steady disruption makes her uneasy about simpler bolt-together systems, and AGI in two or five years alarms her because she won't change trade at her age. Her plan is to cut costs, lean on her parents and chase awkward repair work. With ten years her worry moves to her children's futures.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because her gang and her husband's garage would both be hit with only two weeks of savings.
whatWouldHelp: Time, and help with the mortgage so the bank waits a few months while she finds other work.
